soil-env-237.title: Pesticides: millions of tonnes that mostly miss their mark
soil-env-237.text: In 2023 the world's farms applied 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients, double the 1990 figure. That works out to 2.40 kg on every hectare of cropland. A pesticide is any chemical or biological agent used to deter, incapacitate or kill pests. The family includes herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides. Herbicides, the weed killers, are the most common, at about 50% of all use worldwide. Most of the spray never reaches a pest. Over 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides end up elsewhere, in air, water and soil. Persistence once made this worse. The Stockholm Convention banned long-lived pesticides such as {{ref:soil-env-005}}, which has a soil half-life of 2–15 years and still turns up in people. Modern pesticides must be degradable. Halogens in a molecule slow aerobic breakdown, and binding to soil slows a pesticide's movement but also hides it from the microbes that would break it down. Pests fight back too. They evolve resistance, which prompts new products or higher doses, and more pollution.

soil-env-249.title: Environmental remediation: remove it, treat it or wall it in
soil-env-249.text: Before a polluted site can be built on again, it often has to be cleaned. Environmental remediation is that cleanup: removing, treating or containing hazardous substances in soil, groundwater, sediment and other media. It is the practical answer to {{ref:soil-env-001}}. Developers may even get incentives to clean up voluntarily. Regulations govern the work. Where no standards exist, a risk assessment of harm to people and ecosystems decides instead, and Europe often uses the Dutch standards. The simplest method is excavation, which can mean hauling soil to a regulated landfill or aerating it to release volatile organic compounds, or VOCs. Sometimes the contamination stays put. Barrier walls, built by deep soil mixing, jet grouting, freezing or slurry walls, contain contaminants instead of removing them.

soil-env-242.title: Groundwater pollution: how a spill becomes a plume
soil-env-242.text: A leak at a petrol station can surface years later in a spring. Groundwater pollution is the contamination of {{ref:soil-phys-203}} by pollutants released to the ground, or by unwanted natural constituents, that reach an {{ref:soil-phys-201}}. The sources are many: on-site sanitation, landfill leachate, leaking sewers, petrol stations, fracking and over-applied fertilizer. Nature adds arsenic and fluoride. A pollutant often spreads through the aquifer as a plume and can reach wells, seeps and springs. Diffusion, adsorption, precipitation and decay govern its travel, so analysis weighs soil, geology and hydrogeology. The subsurface can be a reliable natural barrier, but only under favorable conditions. Karst limestone and faults give contaminants quick routes. Some pollutants change on the way: chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene partly decompose into dichloroethylene and vinyl chloride. Nitrate is the most common chemical contaminant of the world's groundwater, and it does not degrade where oxygen is plentiful. Prevention means monitoring, land zoning and careful siting of sanitation. Once a well is polluted, the choices are point-of-use treatment, remediation or abandonment.

soil-env-235.title: Agricultural pollution: what farms leave behind
soil-env-235.text: A 2021 FAO study estimated that farming throws away 10 million tons of plastic a year. Sheeting, mulch and storage bags carry much of it into soil. Agricultural pollution is the full set of farming byproducts, living and nonliving, that contaminate or degrade ecosystems or harm people. It ranges from discharges at a single point to diffuse pollution spread across whole landscapes, and into the air. The pollutants include sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts. They reach lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater. Poor practice drives much of it: badly run animal feeding operations, overgrazing, plowing, and too much fertilizer or pesticide applied at the wrong time. Persistent herbicides such as 2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years, and pesticides build up in animals that eat contaminated pests and soil organisms. Even manure has a hidden load. Manures and biosolids can carry pharmaceuticals and personal care products along with their fertilizer value.

soil-env-257.title: Metal toxicity: when a needed element turns poisonous
soil-env-257.text: In 1956 a release of methylmercury at Minamata alerted the world to bioaccumulation, the buildup of a toxin inside living things. Metal toxicity is harm to plants, animals or people from excessive concentrations of metals. Some metals are double-edged. Copper, iron, manganese and zinc are essential at low levels but toxic at high exposure. Arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and thallium have no biological role in animals at all. Only soluble metal compounds are toxic. Turning them into insoluble forms, or binding them with chelators, molecules that grip metal ions, detoxifies them. Chromium, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead bind strongly to sulfur. They latch onto enzymes through sulfur-bearing thiol groups and block their work. The usual label is shaky: IUPAC calls 'heavy metals' meaningless and misleading, since not all heavy metals are toxic and some toxic metals are not heavy. The sources differ too. Arsenic poisoning comes mainly from naturally arsenic-rich groundwater, lead poisoning from leaded gasoline and plumbing.

soil-env-231.title: Biodegradation: almost everything rots, except elements
soil-env-231.text: Given time, almost every compound breaks down. Elements do not, so heavy metal pollutants never biodegrade. Biodegradation is the breakdown of organic matter by bacteria, fungi and other microbes, the engine of {{ref:soil-bio-115}}. It runs in three stages. Biodeterioration weakens the material, biofragmentation splits its polymer bonds, and assimilation draws the products into microbial cells. Breakdown with oxygen is faster. Without oxygen it also yields methane and shrinks the mass more. Light, water, oxygen, temperature and the compound's availability set the pace, which soil respirometry tests measure through the CO2 microbes release.

soil-env-246.title: Groundwater remediation: cleaning water you cannot see
soil-env-246.text: Between 25 and 40 percent of the world's drinking water comes from boreholes and dug wells. Groundwater remediation is the treatment of that polluted water, either by removing the pollutants or by turning them into harmless products. It applies {{ref:soil-env-249}} to the hidden water described in {{ref:soil-env-242}}. Much of the damage is old. Wastes long dumped on land percolated down, and fertilizer, pesticides, spills, urban runoff and landfills still add more. The toolkit has three drawers. Biological methods include adding microbes ({{ref:soil-env-032}}), bioventing, biosparging, phytoremediation and {{ref:soil-env-247}}. Chemical methods include precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation and surfactants. Physical methods include {{ref:soil-env-250}}, {{ref:soil-env-240}} and dual-phase extraction. Most treatments combine several technologies.

soil-env-259.title: Ecotoxicology: following a poison through an ecosystem
soil-env-259.text: The animals at the top of a food web often suffer most from a pollutant they never touched. Toxicants move up through what each creature eats and accumulate along the way. Ecotoxicology studies how toxic chemicals affect organisms, populations and ecosystems, joining toxicology with ecology. It spans every level from molecules to whole ecosystems. Environmental toxicology, by contrast, centres on organisms, especially human health. Death is not the only harm. Sublethal doses can impair movement or feeding, which shifts competition and the balance between predators and prey. Diversity helps: species-rich communities recover from contamination more readily than poorer ones. The field's findings help predict and prevent damage from {{ref:soil-env-001}}, and show how to restore ecosystem services where harm is done.

soil-env-241.title: Arsenic in well water: a poisoning hidden underground
soil-env-241.text: From the 1970s, millions of tube wells were sunk in Bangladesh. They caused one of the largest mass poisonings. Arsenic contamination of groundwater is pollution, often natural, by high concentrations of arsenic in deeper aquifer water. A 2007 study found over 137 million people in more than 70 countries were probably affected. In Bangladesh the natural contamination was discovered in 1993. Chemistry explains the source. Organic matter in aquifer sediments creates anaerobic conditions, with a low {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Microbes then dissolve iron oxides and release the arsenic bound to them, so arsenic-rich water is often iron-rich. The arsenic occurs as arsenite and arsenate, both soluble; arsenite is somewhat more acutely toxic. Depth matters. In the Ganges Delta the affected wells are mostly 20 to 100 meters deep, and deeper water meets older sediments already stripped of arsenic. The WHO recommends a limit of 10 μg/L, often unattainable because arsenic is hard to remove. Irrigating with this water may add significantly to the arsenic in people's food.

soil-env-220.title: DNAPLs: heavy liquids that sink out of reach
soil-env-220.text: Some pollutants sink straight through groundwater. A dense non-aqueous phase liquid, or DNAPL, is denser than water and does not dissolve in it. Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene, PCBs, some PFAS and some pesticides are examples. Spilled in quantity, DNAPLs drop below the water table and stop only at clay or tight bedrock. That makes them hard to find and clean up. They flow down the slope of that layer, even against the groundwater's flow. A pool keeps dissolving slowly, feeding plumes for years. Where removal is impractical, containment may be the only option.

soil-env-227.title: In situ chemical reduction: iron that disarms solvents
soil-env-227.text: Plain iron metal can clean up some of the most stubborn solvents. In situ chemical reduction lowers contaminant levels by injecting chemical reductants, or placing them in a plume's path, at the site itself. It mirrors {{ref:soil-chem-131}} and treats compounds that resist natural breakdown. Zero-valent iron is the main reductant, used against trichloroethylene and {{ref:soil-env-255}}. On iron surfaces, electrons from the metal, iron released by corrosion or hydrogen strip chlorine from halocarbons. It is often built as a permeable reactive barrier, a trench of iron, though nanoscale iron can be injected directly.

soil-env-222.title: Phytotoxicity: when chemicals stunt or kill plants
soil-env-222.text: Even fertilizer can poison a crop. Phytotoxicity is any harmful effect of a chemical on plant growth, physiology or metabolism. Effects range from disrupted photosynthesis, water and nutrient uptake, cell division or germination to stunted growth and death. Over-applied fertilizer salts, urea and the ammonia it releases, and poorly humified compost can all do it. Herbicides harm non-target plants through spray drift or through contaminated straw or manure spread on soil. Metals follow two rules. Co, Cu, Fe, Ni and Zn are needed in trace amounts but turn toxic past a threshold; As, Cd and Pb are toxic at any concentration.

soil-env-240.title: Air sparging: bubbling solvents out of groundwater
soil-env-240.text: Air sparging cleans groundwater by blowing bubbles through it. Clean air or gas is pumped through wells below the water table into contaminated saturated soil. The small bubbles turn dissolved volatile organic compounds into vapor and carry them up into the unsaturated soil. There, vacuum points pull the vapors into a {{ref:soil-env-045}} system, and granulated activated carbon treats the off-gas. It suits light gasoline constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene. Heavier fuels such as kerosene and diesel do not respond.

soil-env-255.title: Hexavalent chromium: an industrial carcinogen
soil-env-255.text: Hexavalent chromium is rare in nature but made on a large scale, because virtually all chromium ore is processed through sodium dichromate. The name covers any chromium compound in the +6 {{ref:soil-chem-178}}. Inhaled, it can cause lung cancer, and in drinking water it has been found to cause cancers of the mouth and small intestine. At neutral pH, chromate slips into cells through sulfate channels. Inside, it is reduced to chromium(III), which binds DNA and damages genes. Cleanup uses the same step: water is treated by reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III), which activated sludge can also do.

soil-env-238.title: How pesticides break down, and why traces linger
soil-env-238.text: Every year an estimated 1 to 2.5 million tons of active ingredients are used, a large diffuse chemical input. Pesticide degradation is the transformation of a {{ref:soil-env-237}} into a benign substance compatible with the place where it was applied. On paper it is quick: documented soil half-lives are typically days to weeks. Yet residues turn up everywhere, at ng/liter to low μg/liter levels. Microbes do most of the work, through {{ref:soil-env-231}}. Chemical reactions and sunlight add smaller shares. Sunlight's reach is tiny, though, since photochemistry penetrates only submillimeter layers of soil. Underground, redox gradients in soils, sediments and aquifers often decide which reactions are possible. Some microbes are specialists. Bacteria able to cleave glyphosate's stable carbon–phosphorus bond are widespread, and bacterial enzymes in soil strip chlorine from atrazine to make hydroxyatrazine. In groundwater, by contrast, pesticides persist for decades. One explanation is that microbial breakdown stalls at very low concentrations in nutrient-poor settings. Isotopes offer proof that breakdown is happening. Microbes prefer the lighter carbon-12, so a rising 13C/12C ratio in the remaining parent compound is direct evidence of degradation.

soil-env-262.title: In situ bioremediation: cleaning soil where it lies
soil-env-262.text: Digging up polluted soil spreads risk and costs money. In situ bioremediation avoids both by treating the material where it lies. It is {{ref:soil-env-023}} carried out at the site, with microbes that are introduced or fed with nutrients. It treats soils and groundwater polluted by hydrocarbons, chlorinated compounds, nitrates and toxic metals. Left alone, it is one mechanism of natural attenuation. Accelerated forms add nutrients or an electron donor to grow a target microbe, or add microbes outright, which is bioaugmentation. Oxygen supply is often what limits its speed and success. Compared with treatment off site, it costs less and carries less risk of cross-contamination.

soil-env-253.title: Entomoremediation: insects that eat their way through pollution
soil-env-253.text: Insects can clean soil. Entomoremediation is a form of {{ref:soil-env-023}} that uses fly larvae, beetles, ants and {{ref:soil-bio-212}} to decontaminate it. It relies on hardy saprophytic larvae, which feed on dead matter and store toxic heavy metals in their bodies. Black soldier fly larvae have cut the dry weight of a polluted substrate by 49%. They concentrate cadmium with a bioaccumulation factor of 5.6.

soil-env-252.title: Nanoremediation: tiny particles with huge surfaces
soil-env-252.text: Nanoremediation fights pollution with particles too small to see. It uses nano-sized reactive agents to degrade or lock up contaminants in soil or groundwater. The particles are injected in situ or used in pump-and-treat systems. They break down organic pollutants through redox reactions, or adsorb metals such as lead and arsenic. Most field work has used nano zero-valent iron, the same reductant as {{ref:soil-env-227}}. Their large surface per unit mass makes them react fast. It also makes them clump or react with soil particles, limiting how far they spread.

soil-env-250.title: Pump and treat: fast at first, then stubborn
soil-env-250.text: Pump and treat is one of the most widely used ways to clean groundwater. Contaminated water is pumped to the surface and purified, usually through vessels of an adsorbent such as activated carbon. It can quickly cut high concentrations. The last traces are harder. Contaminants keep trading between soil and water by {{ref:soil-chem-145}} and release, so the low levels standards demand are hard to reach. Being slow and expensive, it works best to control the groundwater's flow and stop a release from spreading.

soil-env-251.title: Solidification and stabilization: locking pollutants in place
soil-env-251.text: Some cleanups leave the pollution in the ground but pin it down. Solidification and stabilization mixes a binder into contaminated soil to stop or slow contaminants from moving. Stabilization adds reagents that make them chemically more stable. Solidification locks them in a solid product that air and rain cannot reach. Uptake is slow. Cheap landfill disposal competes with it, and doubts linger over durability, later release and liability for what stays on site. CO2 emissions from the cement it uses are a growing obstacle.

soil-env-254.title: Surfactant flushing: washing heavy solvents from aquifers
soil-env-254.text: Surfactant enhanced aquifer remediation washes an aquifer much as soap washes a greasy pan. A surfactant solution is pumped from injection wells through the contaminated zone to extraction wells. Surfactants make contaminants stuck to saturated soil, or pooled as a {{ref:soil-env-220}}, more mobile and soluble. Extracted water is treated above ground, and the surfactants, non-toxic and biodegradable, are reused. It is used most often on DNAPLs such as trichloroethylene, often as a first step before in situ oxidation or bioremediation.

soil-env-245.title: Mapping which aquifers pollution can reach
soil-env-245.text: Not every aquifer is equally exposed. Shallow unconfined aquifers are most at risk because fewer layers filter contaminants, while the unsaturated zone above can slow or remove pathogens. Aquifer vulnerability mapping overlays maps of such physical factors to show where pollution would reach groundwater most easily. The GOD method uses groundwater confinement, overlying strata and depth to groundwater. EPA's {{ref:soil-env-049}} uses seven factors, including soil media and the impact of the unsaturated zone. Hydrogeologists still disagree on one basic point: whether to rate vulnerability once for all contaminants or separately for each pollutant.

soil-env-243.title: Geogenic contamination: when the rocks poison the water
soil-env-243.text: Not all polluted groundwater has a human culprit. Geogenic contamination arises naturally, from geological processes such as {{ref:soil-found-052}}. Arsenic and fluoride are the most widespread offenders; salinity, iron, manganese, uranium, radon and chromium matter more locally. WHO tests found 20% of 25,000 Bangladesh boreholes above 50 μg/L arsenic. High fluoride usually reflects fluoride minerals such as fluorite and a lack of calcium in the aquifer. Above 1.5 mg/L it can cause dental fluorosis, a mottling of the teeth.

soil-env-244.title: How soil filters germs from latrine seepage
soil-env-244.text: Soil is a slow but real germ filter. Liquid leaching from pit latrines and septic tanks loses pathogens as it trickles through the unsaturated soil, as they die off or stick to grains. Travel time to the well matters most. Most, but not all, pathogens die within 50 days underground. Soil type, aquifer type and distance change the result, and long heavy rain can flush the zone and open fast pathways. The topsoil, the most biologically active layer, removes the most. A general guideline sets a pit's base at least 2 m above groundwater and 30 m from a water source.

soil-env-233.title: Neutralizing acid mine drainage
soil-env-233.text: Treating {{ref:soil-bio-059}} means neutralizing its acid and stripping out dissolved metals. Crushed limestone is the cheapest neutralizer, but its grains get armored with gypsum and an iron–aluminium film that stops them dissolving. Lime slurry instead raises the water to about pH 9, where most toxic metals settle out as sludge. Constructed wetlands are cheap. Their sediment bacteria turn sulfate into sulfide, which binds and drops heavy metals, though only limited loads. Sulfate-reducing bacteria in reactors also yield bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid.

soil-env-234.title: Yellow boy, the orange stain of mine water
soil-env-234.text: Streams below old mines often run a lurid yellow-orange. The color is yellow boy, the iron(III) hydroxide that settles out when the pH of {{ref:soil-bio-059}} rises above 3. Other iron compounds, including oxyhydroxides and sulfates such as jarosite, can form too. All of them discolor water and smother life on the streambed. Their formation releases more hydrogen ions, which lowers the pH further. Very rich deposits can even be recovered as pigment.

soil-env-230.title: Thermal desorption: baking pollutants out of soil
soil-env-230.text: Cooking pollutants out of soil leaves surprisingly little behind. Removing 500 mg/kg of organics from 20,000 tons of soil yields under 3,000 US gallons of liquid, less than one tank truck. Thermal desorption heats contaminated soil until its contaminants evaporate, then collects or destroys them. A system has a desorber and an offgas treatment system, and it is not incineration. Rotary cylinders and heated screws are common desorbers. Used at 69 US Superfund sites through FY2000, it counts as a permanent remedy at competitive cost, unlike stabilization, which leaves contaminants on site.

soil-env-221.title: LNAPLs: pollutants that float on the water table
soil-env-221.text: Some pollutants float. A light non-aqueous phase liquid, or LNAPL, is a hydrocarbon that does not dissolve in water and is lighter than it. Benzene, toluene and xylene are examples. Once an LNAPL soaks into the ground, it stops at the {{ref:soil-water-247}} and spreads there as a separate layer. That buoyancy is good news. Sitting on top, LNAPLs are easier and cheaper to find and remove than {{ref:soil-env-220}}, which sink.

soil-env-219.title: Biosorption: dead cells that grab metals
soil-env-219.text: Dead bacteria can outperform living ones at catching metal. In one test, dead Bacillus sphaericus cells took up 13–20% more chromium than live cells. Biosorption is a passive process in which certain biomass binds contaminants such as heavy metals to its cell surface. Unlike bioaccumulation, it needs no living, respiring organism and no energy. The binding is reversible, and pH, biomass concentration and competing metal ions shape it. Cheap wastes such as eggshells, peat, fungi, seaweed and crab shells work, at about a tenth the cost of ion-exchange resins.
